title: The Education Gadfly Weekly, Volume 26, Number 37 September 17, 2026
author: Thomas B. Fordham Institute
source: The Education Gadfly Weekly, Thomas B. Fordham Institute (fordhaminstitute.org),
summary: This issue of the Fordham Institute's Education Gadfly Weekly curates three new commentaries, two study reviews, one research report, and three pieces from the previous week, each introduced with a short editorial summary. The featured commentaries argue that the backlash against college for all should not become a new one-size-fits-all rule (Matthew Carr), that student AI use raises moral questions of honesty and effort that school rules alone cannot resolve (Alicia Anderson), and that the fastest way to expand private school choice is to fill empty seats in existing, largely Catholic, schools (Kathleen Porter-Magee). The reviews cover NCES's mapping of state proficiency standards onto the NAEP scale (Amber Northern), which finds most state bars below NAEP Proficient, and a Nature Communications study showing childhood investment gaps are smaller than thought and largest before school entry (Kendall Rogers). The research slot promotes Brian Fitzpatrick's survey report on high school technology, AI cheating, and grade inflation, with the editors concluding that technology is not the enemy but high schools need far less of it. The issue closes with ICYMI links to Mike Petrilli on AI bans, Dale Chu on the education legacy of 9/11, and Aaron Garth Smith on school finance reform, giving the week a combined focus on standards, technology, and policy.
points: Carr's lead piece reframes post-secondary advising: grades predict college completion but cannot show whether college or another pathway leaves a particular student better off.
Anderson's commentary shifts the AI debate from device access to moral formation, urging parents to lead conversations about whether and how the technology should be used.
Porter-Magee points to Florida as evidence that filling unused seats in existing schools is faster and cheaper than building new ones as choice programs expand.
Northern's review of NCES data finds most state proficiency thresholds still fall below NAEP's, framing the result as a measure of how much room remains to raise expectations.

The featured Fitzpatrick report concludes that misused school devices are nearly as distracting as personal phones and, combined with AI misuse and grade inflation, have hollowed out the high school experience.
quotes: Academic performance in high school can predict whether students will succeed in college, but it cannot tell us whether college—or another pathway—will leave a particular student better off.
AI use is about far more than children accessing Gemini on their school Chromebooks. It raises hard questions about honesty, effort, judgment, and the value of doing difficult work.
That makes sense in places where capacity is scarce, but in other locales, a faster and more cost-effective way to serve more families is to fill unused seats in existing schools.
This is most useful in showing leaders how much room there is to keep raising expectations—and how low current expectations are for many schools and students.

Children from different racial and socioeconomic backgrounds receive unequal investments of money, other public resources, and family time, but a new study finds that those disparities are smaller than estimates reported in previous research.

His findings show that school-issued devices are often misused, making them nearly as distracting as students’ personal cell phones. Combine that with unethical use of AI and rampant grade inflation, and we’ve seriously hollowed out the American high school experience.
Technology isn’t the enemy here. But the findings suggest we need far less of it in today’s high schools.
